sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Kalki** (*kalki*) ​— The ‌Tenth Avatāra, the ‌End of ​the Kali Yuga ​· The ​avatāra yet to ​come — ​the tenth and ‌final avatāra ​of Viṣṇu, who ​appears at the ‌end of ​the Kali Yuga ‌riding a ​white horse to ‌destroy unrighteousness ​and restore the ​age of ​truth — belongs ​to the ​Sanskrit tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued under the ‌domain "Prophecy, ​Renewal, Avatar of ‌Vishnu". The ​name means "The ‌avatāra yet ​to come — ‌the tenth ​and final avatāra ​of Viṣṇu, ‌who appears at ‌the end of ‌the Kali ​Yuga riding a ​white horse ‌to destroy unrighteousness ​and restore ​the age of ‌truth"[^1].

**Kalki** ​is Vishnu’s final ​descent: the ‌warrior on the ​white horse ‌who will come ​when the ​Kali Yuga chokes ​on its ​own corruption — ‌sword drawn, ‌comet-marked, born in ​a village ‌to a Brahmin ​named Viṣṇuyaśas — ​to end ‌the age, punish ‌the wicked, ‌and restart the ‌world’s golden ​wheel. He is ‌the only ​deity in this ​pantheon whose ​myth is a ‌prophecy.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records the canonical ​scholarly spelling ​**Kalki** and serves ‌its temple ​at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/kalki/). ​The displayed ​form is ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description computed from ‌the displayed ​form itself. The ‌plain ASCII form ​*kalki* contains ‌the same letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics or special ​encoding is ​claimed. The work ​here is ‌consistent citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, and ​cultural context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Devanagari ​as **कल्कि**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"The ​avatāra yet ‌to ​come — ​the ‌tenth and ​final avatāra ‌of ​Viṣṇu, who ‌appears ​at the ​end ​of the ​Kali ​Yuga riding ‌a white ​horse ‌to destroy ​unrighteousness ‌and restore ​the ‌age of ​truth"[^1].

‌The canonical ​spelling **Kalki** ​matches ‌the conventional ‌scholarly ‌romanization. The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*kalki* ​contains the ​same letters, ‌so ​no lost ​diacritics ‌or encoding ​transition ‌is claimed. ​The ​editorial work ​is to ​fix ‌one reviewed ‌reference ​spelling, preserve ‌capitalization ​and provenance, ​and ‌keep the ‌original evidence ‌visible. ‌The displayed ​form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— ​a description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed form ​itself.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- **k** ​→ ​**K** — ‌Same
- ​**a** → ‌**a** — ​Short ‌/a/
- **l** ​→ ‌**l** — ‌Same
- ​**k** → ​**k** ​— Same
- ​**i** → ‌**i** ‌— Short ​/i/

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/ˈkɑːlki/** ​— ​Sanskrit (IAST: ‌Kalki).[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

- ​**Kāl-** — ‌Conventionally ​written ‌Kalki; ​the ​name is ​usually ​derived ​from ‌kalikā ​“white horse” ‌or ​from ‌Kali, ​the ‌age he ​ends.
- ‌**-ki** ​— ​The ‌tenth ‌avatāra of ‌Vishnu, ​yet ​to ‌come ​— the ​only ‌future ​god ​in ‌the lexicon.

​For ‌the ​modern ​speaker, ​the closest ​approximation ‌is: ‌“KAHL-kee”

​Kindred ‌and historical ​forms ​of ‌the ‌name:

- ‌**Kalkin** ‌— in ​some ‌Purāṇic ​lists
- ​**the** ​— White ‌Horse ​of ​the ​world’s ‌end

A ​prophecy ​made ​flesh ‌in ​text: the ‌god ​who ‌has ​not ‌yet been ‌born, ​scheduled ​for ​the ​end of ‌the ‌Kali ​Yuga.

sections.body:
**Kalki** ​is Vishnu’s ‌final descent: ‌the ​warrior on ​the ​white horse ​who will ​come ‌when the ​Kali Yuga ​chokes ‌on its ​own corruption ‌— ​sword drawn, ‌comet-marked, ​born in ​a village ​to ​a Brahmin ​named Viṣṇuyaśas ‌— ​to end ‌the age, ​punish ‌the wicked, ​and ‌restart the ​world’s golden ‌wheel. ​He is ​the only ‌deity ‌in this ‌pantheon whose ​myth ​is a ‌prophecy.[^1]

### ​The White ​Horse

Devadatta, ‌the ​winged white ​steed, given ‌by ​Śiva; Kalki ‌rides from ​Śambhala ​at the ​age’s ​end.

### The ‌Sword of ‌the ​Age

Ratnamaru, ‌the jewelled ​sword, ​given by ‌the gods ‌— ‌it ends ‌the ​Kali Yuga ‌as a ​blade ​ends a ​lie.

### Born ‌in ​Śambhala

His ​village, Śambhala, ​waits ‌hidden; when ​dharma’s ​four legs ​shrink to ‌one, ​he is ‌born there.

### ​The ‌Restarter of ​Time

After ‌the ‌sword, the ​restart: ​Kalki inaugurates ​the next ​Kṛta ‌Yuga — ‌death midwifing ​rebirth.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Kalki ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed statement ‌about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The ​White Horse** ​— ​Devadatta, ​the ‌winged ​white steed, ‌given ​by ‌Śiva; ​Kalki ‌rides from ​Śambhala ‌at ​the ​age’s ‌end.
- ‌**The Sword ‌of ​the ​Age** ‌— ​Ratnamaru, the ​jewelled ‌sword, ​given ​by ‌the gods ​— ‌it ​ends ​the ​Kali Yuga ​as ‌a ‌blade ​ends ‌a lie.
- ​**Born ​in ‌Śambhala** ‌— ‌His ‌village, Śambhala, ​waits ‌hidden; ​when ​dharma’s ​four legs ‌shrink ​to ​one, ​he ‌is born ​there.
- ​**The ​Restarter ‌of ​Time** — ‌After ​the ‌sword, ​the ‌restart: Kalki ‌inaugurates ​the ​next ​Kṛta ​Yuga — ‌death ‌midwifing ​rebirth.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The Kalki ​myth is the Purāṇic ‌eschaton: the prophecies ‌of the Kali ​Yuga’s decay — merchants ​as kings, wealth ​as virtue, fathers ​feared by sons — ​are the diagnosis, ‌and Kalki is ​the cure. He appears ​in the latest ‌strata of the Mahābhārata ​and the Purāṇas ‌as the tenth ​and final avatāra, the ‌one Vishnu keeps ​in reserve for ​the world’s last night.[^1]

### ​The Prophecy of ​the Horse (Mahābhārata ​3.191)

The earliest Kalki-passage ‌names the signs: ​when time decays, a ‌being of immense ​power will be ‌born to a family ​of Brahmins, swift ‌as thought, his ​hand a sword, his ‌steed white as ​milk, blazing like ​a comet. The passage ‌is embedded in ‌the epic’s cosmological books ‌as Vishnu’s promise ​to the tormented ​earth.[^2]

### The Full Biography ‌(Kalki Purāṇa)

The ​eponymous Purāṇa tells ​it whole: the child ‌Kalki, mocked by ​the corrupt, learns ​the Vedas from Paraśurāma ‌himself, marries the ​princess Padmāvatī by the ‌sword-contest, and rides ​out against the ​mleccha kings. His campaigns ​purify the world; ​the wicked fall ‌to his blade and ‌the earth’s burden ​lifts at last.

### ‌The Diagnosis of the ​Age (Kali Yuga ​Doctrines)

The Purāṇic Kali-Yuga ‌lists read like ‌satire: rulers will ‌be thieves, vows will ‌be sold, the ​low will govern ‌the high. Kalki is ​the answer to ​this audit — ​not a reformer but ‌an ending. The ​theology is cyclical: he ​destroys the age ​as a farmer ‌burns the stubble, so ​the next golden ​age can be ​sown.

### The Expected One ‌(Living Traditions)

Kalki ​remains expected: in ‌Śambhala-legend — Tibetan Buddhism ​adopted the hidden ‌kingdom wholesale — and ​in popular Hinduism, ‌where every generation ‌finds the Kali Yuga’s ​signs fulfilled. He ​is the only ​god in this pantheon ​whose temple is ‌the future, and ‌whose devotees wait rather ​than celebrate.
